tagline: A content calendar that suggests what to post, not just when.
verdictSummary: Loomly's difference from the other schedulers is that it arrives with something to say: a calendar seeded with holidays, awareness days and trending events relevant to your niche, so an empty week comes with prompts rather than a blank composer. That is a maintained dataset plus a matching rule, and the dataset is the part you inherit responsibility for. The publishing half is the same one-network-at-a-time story every scheduler in this catalogue tells.
coreLoopDIY: Keep a content calendar seeded with dates that matter to your audience, turn a suggested date into a draft with one click, and publish approved posts to one connected network.
whatYouLose: the maintained calendar of events and trending topics
every network beyond the one you got API approval for
the shared asset library with brand rules attached
the multi-stage approval workflow for a team
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of a content calendar is not scheduling, it is having something worth scheduling. A dataset of relevant dates updated every month is the actual product.
notes: The idea-generation angle: the other social entries in this catalogue cover metrics, approval workflow, bulk import and single-platform publishing, and none of them address the blank calendar.
prompt:
Build a social content calendar whose distinguishing feature is that it suggests what to post about.

Event dataset: a YAML file of dated prompts, each with a date or a recurrence rule, a title, a short description, a set of tags identifying which niches it suits, and a relevance weight. Ship a small seed set — public holidays for a chosen country, a handful of widely observed awareness days — and make clear in the README that keeping this current is the user's ongoing job and is the real cost of running this yourself. Support importing an ICS calendar as an additional source, so a user can pull in an industry event calendar somebody else maintains.

Calendar view: a month grid showing scheduled posts and, on empty days, suggestions drawn from the dataset filtered to the user's declared tags and ranked by weight. A suggestion is dismissible, and a dismissed one does not return that year. Clicking a suggestion opens the composer pre-filled with its title and description as a starting note, not as post text — the tool prompts, it does not write.

Evergreen prompts: alongside dated events, a pool of undated content prompts the user maintains ("answer a customer question", "show work in progress", "share a result with a number in it"), surfaced on days with no dated suggestion. This is what keeps a calendar full in a quiet month.

Composer and publishing: character count against the connected network's real limit, media validation for size and aspect ratio before scheduling, and a week-view queue. Connect exactly one network through its documented OAuth flow, publish through a background worker with idempotency keys, store the returned post ID, and surface failures with the platform's own error text.

Asset library: local media with tags and a usage note per asset, plus a per-asset record of which posts have used it and when, so the same image is not posted twice in a month.

History: every published post archived with its text, media and date, searchable, so a good post from last year can be found and reworked.

Out of scope: additional networks, scraping, analytics on published posts, team approval chains, and any AI generation of post text.

faq.q: Can I import my Loomly calendar?
faq.a: Posts export as CSV, so text and dates come across. The event and idea calendar is Loomly's own data and does not export at all, which is exactly the part you would most want — building your seed file is the real migration work here.

faq.q: Why not have a model generate the post ideas?
faq.a: Because generic prompts are worse than none. A model asked for content ideas produces the same twenty suggestions for every business, whereas a maintained list of dates that actually matter to your audience is specific by construction. The prompt keeps the tool prompting rather than writing.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: A small VPS with PostgreSQL, five to ten dollars a month, plus local media storage. The ongoing cost is not money — it is the half hour each month spent keeping the event file current, which is precisely the work the subscription covers.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Relevance decay. A seeded event file is useful in January and stale by June unless somebody maintains it, and the honest failure mode of this build is a calendar that quietly stops suggesting anything worth posting.
